newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's L'Oreal reports higher 1996 profits.
newsitem.headline: France's L'Oreal reports higher 1996 profits.

text.p: French cosmetics giant L'Oreal confirmed on Wednesday that profits rose 10 percent last year on sales growth helped by the acquisition of U.S.-based Maybelline.
L'Oreal issued an upbeat outlook for 1997.

It said operating profit jumped 17.6 percent to 7.3 billion francs ($1.3 billion) in 1996, boosted by gains in both cosmetics and pharmaceutical activities through its 56 percent stake in drug company Synthelabo.

But a rise in finance charges due partly to the $760 million Maybelline acquisition trimmed profit growth on the bottom line. Net attributable profit excluding capital gains and losses increased by 10.3 percent to 3.7 billion francs.

L'Oreal reported its results provisionally in February but its stock got a small boost from the announcement of a 15.8 percent dividend increase to 14 francs and Chairman Lindsay Owen-Jones' forecast for a higher profit this year.
"If rates hold steady from here to the end of the year, it would seem possible to forecast double-digit profit growth, which is our goal today," Owen-Jones told a news conference.
The share closed 1.11 percent higher at 1,908 francs.
L'Oreal's cosmetics business, which accounted for 81 percent of total sales of 60.3 billion francs, grew by 13 percent last year.
"Our cosmetics business grew nearly twice as fast as the global market and represents market share of 12 to 13 percent," said finance director Pascal Castres Saint Martin.
L'Oreal's brands range from the upscale Lancome and Biotherm lines to Redken hair products, the Vichy line sold in pharmacies and the Gemey and Jade mass-market brands.
With the acquisition of Maybelline, intended to spearhead expansion into emerging markets, L'Oreal further reduced its dependence on the slow-growing European market.

For the first time, it generated more than 40 percent of sales outside Europe in 1996. L'Oreal is growing in eastern Europe -- it has a factory in Poland and plans to build one in Russia -- as well as southeast Asia and Latin America.
The group's results were helped by a 19.7 percent jump in net attributable profit at Synthelabo.
Owen-Jones said L'Oreal's stake in the company was a handsome investment and the group was not under pressure to decide quickly whether to remain in the pharmaceuticals business or pull out.
